ref-methods.prompt: The most examinable table in the course, because it is short, factual and easy to mark.
ref-methods.solution:
MethodPurposeHas a body?Safe?Idempotent?
GETRetrieve a resourceNoYesYes
POSTCreate a resource, or submit data for processingYesNoNo
PUTReplace a resource entirelyYesNoYes
PATCHModify part of a resourceYesNoNo
DELETERemove a resourceUsually notNoYes
HEADLike GET but returns headers onlyNoYesYes
OPTIONSAsk which methods a resource supportsNoYesYes

Safe means the request does not change server state. Idempotent means making the same request many times has the same effect as making it once. DELETE is idempotent even though it changes state, because deleting the same resource twice leaves the same result: gone. POST is not, because posting twice creates two records. That is exactly why a browser warns before resubmitting a form.

GET against POST, the classic comparison

GETPOST
Data goes inThe URL query string, visibleThe request body, not shown in the URL
Length limitLimited by URL lengthEffectively unlimited
Cached and bookmarkedYesNo
In browser historyYes, with its dataNo
Use forRetrieving, searching, filteringLogging in, uploading, creating records

Note the security point carefully: POST is not encrypted, it merely keeps the data out of the URL and out of the browser history. Only HTTPS provides confidentiality. Saying "POST is secure" loses the mark; saying "POST hides data from the URL, but only HTTPS encrypts it" earns it.

ref-status.prompt: Learn the five classes, then the specific codes inside them. A question usually asks for the classes plus three or four named codes.
ref-status.solution:
ClassMeaningCodes worth naming
1xxInformational, the request was received and is continuing100 Continue
2xxSuccess200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xxRedirection, further action is needed301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified
4xxClient error, the request was faulty400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorised, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 429 Too Many Requests
5xxServer error, the request was valid but the server failed500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable

The distinction examiners like: 401 means not authenticated, so the server does not know who you are and a login would help. 403 means not authorised, so the server knows exactly who you are and you still may not have it, and logging in again will not help. The other pairing is 4xx against 5xx: 4xx blames the client, 5xx blames the server.

ref-mobile.prompt: The central comparison of the mobile half, and close to a guaranteed question. Learn it as a table so you can answer "compare X and Y under stated criteria" whichever pair is named.
ref-mobile.solution:
NativeCross-platformHybridProgressive web app
Built withKotlin or Java for Android, Swift for iOSReact Native, FlutterWeb technologies inside a native shell, such as Ionic or CordovaHTML, CSS and JavaScript, run in the browser
PerformanceBestNear nativeLower, runs in a web viewLowest
Device featuresFull accessMost, through bridges and pluginsThrough pluginsLimited by what the browser exposes
CodebasesOne per platformOneOneOne
DistributionApp storeApp storeApp storeA URL; installable from the browser
Cost and timeHighestModerateLowLowest
OfflineYesYesYesYes, via a service worker

The one line to close any comparison answer with: choose native when performance or deep device access dominates, such as a game or a camera application; choose cross-platform when reaching both platforms quickly with one team matters more; choose a PWA when reach and cost matter most and the app is largely content and forms. A recommendation, justified, is what turns a table into an answer.

The three things that define a progressive web app: a service worker for offline caching and background work, a web app manifest giving it a name and icon so it installs to the home screen, and it must be served over HTTPS. Name all three.

ref-stack.prompt: A short definition question that appears constantly, and the vocabulary the rest of the course depends on.
ref-stack.solution:
Front end (client side)Back end (server side)
Runs onThe user's browser or deviceThe server
Responsible forPresentation, layout, interaction, client-side validationBusiness logic, data storage, authentication, authorisation
LanguagesHTML, CSS, JavaScriptPHP, Python, Java, Node.js, C#
FrameworksReact, Vue, Angular, Bootstrap, TailwindLaravel, Django, Express, Spring
Can the user see and change it?Yes: it is downloaded to their machineNo: it never leaves the server

The last row is the one that carries a real mark, so state it explicitly: client-side validation is a convenience, never a security control. The user can disable JavaScript, edit the page or call the API directly, so every check must be repeated on the server. Validate on the client for a fast, kind user experience, and on the server because that is the only place it counts.

Full stack means working on both. A framework imposes a structure and calls your code, while a library is code you call; that distinction, often phrased as inversion of control, is worth one sentence if the term comes up.

t1.prompt: "Describe what happens when a user types a URL and presses enter" is the single most common opening question in this course, because it lets the examiner test six topics at once.
t1.solution:
The full sequence

  1. URL parsing. The browser splits the URL into protocol, host, port, path and query string.
  2. DNS resolution. The host name is resolved to an IP address, checking the browser cache, then the operating system cache, then a DNS server.
  3. TCP connection. A connection is opened to that address on the port, usually 80 or 443, by the three way handshake.
  4. TLS handshake, if the scheme is HTTPS: certificates are exchanged and verified and a session key agreed.
  5. HTTP request. The browser sends a request line, headers and possibly a body.
  6. Server processing. The server routes the request, runs the application code, perhaps queries a database, and builds a response.
  7. HTTP response. A status line, headers and the body come back.
  8. Rendering. The browser parses the HTML into the DOM, fetches the CSS, images and scripts it references, builds the render tree, lays it out and paints it.

The anatomy of a URL

https://greyat-study-guide.vercel.app:443/csc311?topic=http#t1
└─┬─┘   └──────────┬──────────────────┘└┬┘└──┬──┘└────┬────┘└┬┘
scheme          host                  port  path    query  fragment

The fragment, everything after the #, is never sent to the server. It is handled entirely by the browser, which is why an anchor link jumps within a page without a new request. That detail catches people out and is worth a mark on its own.

Request and response structure

Request                          Response
-------                          --------
GET /csc311 HTTP/1.1             HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Host: example.com                Content-Type: text/html
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0          Content-Length: 4821
Accept: text/html                Set-Cookie: session=abc123
(optional body)                  (body: the HTML document)

Both are: a first line, then headers, then a blank line, then an optional body. Being able to draw that shape is often worth two or three marks.

Drill

  1. Describe what happens when a user enters a URL in a browser. The eight steps above, in order.
  2. Label the parts of a URL. Scheme, host, port, path, query string, fragment, with the note that the fragment stays in the browser.
  3. Describe the structure of an HTTP request and response. Start line, headers, blank line, optional body, with an example of each.
  4. What is the client-server model? An architecture in which a client requests a service and a server provides it, the two communicating over a network by an agreed protocol, with the server holding the shared data and logic and the client handling presentation and input.

t2.prompt: HTTP is stateless: the server keeps no memory of previous requests, and each one is treated as though it came from a stranger. Everything about logins and shopping baskets follows from working around that.
t2.solution:
Statelessness is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight. It makes servers far easier to scale, because any server can handle any request, and it means a crashed server loses nothing that was not already stored.

The three ways state is maintained

MechanismWhere the data livesNotes
CookiesOn the client, sent with every request to that domainSmall, about 4 KB. Can be marked HttpOnly so JavaScript cannot read them, and Secure so they travel only over HTTPS
SessionsOn the server, with only an identifier in a cookieThe data itself is never exposed to the client, so this is the safer default
Tokens, such as JWTOn the client, usually sent in an Authorization headerSelf-contained and signed, so the server need not store anything, which suits APIs and mobile apps

Sessions against tokens is the modern version of this question. A session is stateful on the server, so it can be revoked instantly but requires shared storage across servers. A token is stateless, so it scales freely, but cannot easily be revoked before it expires. That trade-off, revocation against scalability, is the answer.

Browser storage to name alongside cookies: localStorage, which persists until cleared, and sessionStorage, which is cleared when the tab closes. Neither is sent to the server automatically, which is the main difference from a cookie.

Drill

  1. What does it mean that HTTP is stateless, and why is it designed that way? Each request is independent and the server keeps no memory between them; it is designed that way because it makes servers simple to scale and resilient, since no request depends on which server handled the last one.
  2. Differentiate a cookie from a session. A cookie stores data on the client and is sent with every request; a session stores the data on the server and sends only an identifier, so the data is never exposed.
  3. Differentiate localStorage from sessionStorage from cookies. localStorage persists indefinitely, sessionStorage lasts for the tab, and both stay on the client unless code sends them; a cookie is transmitted with every request to its domain automatically.
  4. Why should a session cookie be marked HttpOnly and Secure? HttpOnly stops JavaScript reading it, which blocks a cross-site scripting attack from stealing the session; Secure stops it being sent over plain HTTP, which blocks interception on the network.

t3.prompt: HTML describes the structure and meaning of content, not its appearance. That separation, structure in HTML, presentation in CSS, behaviour in JavaScript, is itself a standard question.
t3.solution:
A minimal document

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
<title>Page title</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Heading</h1>
</body>
</html>

Three lines there are worth explaining if asked. <!doctype html> tells the browser to use standards mode rather than a legacy quirks mode. charset="utf-8" declares the character encoding, without which non-ASCII characters may render as rubbish. The viewport meta tag is what makes a page respond to phone width at all: without it a mobile browser assumes a desktop-width page and zooms out, so every media query you write is ignored.

Semantic elements

ElementMeaning
<header>, <footer>Introductory and closing content for a page or section
<nav>A block of navigation links
<main>The dominant content, one per page
<article>Self-contained content that would make sense on its own
<section>A thematic grouping, normally with a heading
<aside>Tangential content, such as a sidebar
<figure>, <figcaption>An image or diagram with its caption

Why use them instead of <div> everywhere? Three reasons, and give all three: accessibility, since a screen reader can jump straight to <main> or list the headings; search engine optimisation, since crawlers use the structure to judge what matters; and maintainability, since the markup describes itself. A <div> carries no meaning at all, which is precisely when you should use one.

Forms and accessibility

Every input needs a <label> tied to it by for and id, so that clicking the label focuses the field and a screen reader announces it. Use the right input type, namely email, tel, number, date, because on a phone the type chooses the keyboard the user gets. Use required, min, max and pattern for built-in validation, remembering R4: it must still be checked on the server.

Accessibility points worth naming: alt text on every meaningful image and empty alt on decorative ones, headings used in order without skipping levels, sufficient colour contrast, and every interactive control reachable by keyboard.

Drill

  1. What is the role of HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a web page? Structure and meaning, presentation, and behaviour respectively.
  2. Name six semantic HTML5 elements and their purpose, and say why they are preferred to div. The table plus the three reasons.
  3. What is the viewport meta tag and why does a responsive site need it? It tells the mobile browser to use the device width as the layout width; without it the browser assumes a desktop width and scales the page down, so media queries never take effect.
  4. State four things that make a form accessible. A label associated with every input, correct input types, keyboard operability, and clear error messages tied to the field they concern.

t4.prompt: CSS controls presentation. Three things get examined: the box model, the layout systems, and how a page adapts to screen size.
t4.solution:
The box model

Every element is a box of four concentric layers, from the inside out: content, padding, border, margin.

┌─────────────────── margin ───────────────────┐
│  ┌──────────────── border ────────────────┐  │
│  │  ┌───────────── padding ────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │            content               │  │  │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The calculation question: with box-sizing: content-box, the default, a declared width: 200px applies to the content only, so 20px of padding and a 2px border on each side give a total occupied width of 200 + 40 + 4 = 244px. With box-sizing: border-box, the declared width includes padding and border, so the element occupies exactly 200px and the content shrinks to 156px. That is why almost every real stylesheet sets border-box globally.

Layout systems

SystemBest forKey properties
Normal flowOrdinary document contentBlock and inline display
FlexboxOne dimension, a row or a columndisplay:flex, justify-content, align-items, flex-wrap, gap
GridTwo dimensions, rows and columns togetherdisplay:grid, grid-template-columns, grid-gap
PositionTaking an element out of the flowstatic, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky

Specificity, since it explains "why is my style not applying"

From weakest to strongest: element selectors, then class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors, then ID selectors, then inline styles, and finally !important, which overrides everything and should be avoided precisely because it does. Where two rules have equal specificity, the one written later wins. That, and inheritance, is the whole of the cascade.

Responsive design

  • Fluid layouts using percentages, fr units, rem, vw and vh rather than fixed pixels.
  • Media queries applying different rules at different widths: @media (max-width: 600px) { ... }.
  • Flexible images, typically max-width: 100%; height: auto; so an image never overflows its container.
  • Mobile first, meaning the base stylesheet targets the small screen and media queries add complexity for larger ones. This is preferred because the simplest device gets the simplest stylesheet, and because it forces you to decide what actually matters.

Worth saying in a Nigerian context, and it is a genuine engineering point rather than padding: most of your users are on a phone over mobile data, so mobile first and a small page weight are not stylistic preferences but the difference between a site that is used and one that is abandoned while loading.

Drill

  1. Explain the CSS box model and calculate the total width of an element with width 300px, padding 15px, border 3px and margin 10px, under content-box. Content 300 + padding 30 + border 6 = 336px occupied, plus 20px of margin around it.
  2. Differentiate flexbox from grid. Flexbox lays out along one axis at a time and is best for a row or column of items; grid controls rows and columns simultaneously and is best for a whole page or component layout.
  3. What is responsive web design, and state four techniques used to achieve it? Designing one page that adapts to any screen size, using fluid layouts, media queries, flexible images and a mobile first approach.
  4. Explain CSS specificity. The rule for deciding which conflicting declaration wins, ordered element, then class, then ID, then inline, with !important above all; ties are broken by source order.

t5.prompt: The DOM, document object model, is the browser's representation of the page as a tree of objects. JavaScript changes the page by changing that tree, not by editing the HTML file.
t5.solution:
That sentence is the answer to "what is the DOM": it is a programming interface to the document, presenting it as a tree in which every element, attribute and piece of text is a node that a script can read, change, add or remove. The page the user sees reflects the DOM, so changing the DOM changes the page immediately.

The operations to know

// Selecting
document.getElementById("total")
document.querySelector(".card")
document.querySelectorAll("li")
// Changing
el.textContent = "Hello"      // text only, safe
el.innerHTML   = "<b>Hi</b>"  // parses HTML, unsafe with user input
el.classList.add("active")
el.setAttribute("disabled", "")
// Creating
const li = document.createElement("li")
list.appendChild(li)
// Events
button.addEventListener("click", function (e) { ... })

The security note attached to that snippet is examinable in its own right: writing user-supplied text with innerHTML lets an attacker inject a script tag, which is cross-site scripting. textContent escapes everything, so it is the safe default.

Event handling

An event travels in three phases: capturing from the document down to the target, the target phase, then bubbling back up. Bubbling is what makes event delegation possible: attach one listener to a list and it will catch clicks on every item, including items added later, which is far cheaper than a listener per item.

e.preventDefault() stops the browser's default action, such as a form submitting or a link navigating. e.stopPropagation() stops the event travelling further up the tree. They are different things and are often confused.

Synchronous and asynchronous

JavaScript in the browser is single threaded, so a long running synchronous operation freezes the whole page. Anything slow, such as a network request, is therefore asynchronous: it is started, the thread continues, and a callback runs when it completes. The three generations of syntax are callbacks, then promises, then async and await, which is promises written to look synchronous.

// Promise style
fetch("/api/materials")
.then(res => res.json())
.then(data => render(data))
.catch(err => showError(err))
// async/await style, same thing
async function load() {
try {
const res  = await fetch("/api/materials")
const data = await res.json()
render(data)
} catch (err) {
showError(err)
}
}

Drill

  1. What is the DOM? The definition above, with the tree of nodes and the point that changing it changes the rendered page.
  2. Differentiate textContent from innerHTML, and say which is safer. textContent sets plain text and escapes markup; innerHTML parses its argument as HTML, so user input placed there can inject scripts. textContent is the safe default.
  3. Explain event bubbling and event delegation. An event fired on an element travels up through its ancestors; delegation exploits this by placing one listener on a common ancestor to handle events from many descendants, including ones added later.
  4. Why is asynchronous programming necessary in the browser? Because JavaScript runs on a single thread that also handles rendering and input, so a blocking operation such as waiting for a network response would freeze the entire interface until it finished.

t6.prompt: AJAX, asynchronous JavaScript and XML, is the technique of requesting data from the server after the page has loaded and updating part of the page without reloading it. Despite the name, the data is almost always JSON now.
t6.solution:
Why it mattered: before AJAX, every interaction meant a full page reload, so the browser discarded and rebuilt the entire document to change one number. AJAX made web pages behave like applications. That historical sentence is usually what the question is really asking for.

JSON against XML

JSONXML
SyntaxObjects and arrays, like JavaScript literalsNested tags with attributes
VerbosityCompactHeavier, every value wrapped in an open and close tag
ParsingNative in JavaScript, JSON.parseRequires a parser and tree traversal
Data typesString, number, boolean, null, object, arrayEverything is text unless a schema says otherwise
Comments, schemasNo comments; schemas exist but are less usedSupports comments, namespaces and mature schema languages

CORS, which every student meets as a bug first

The same origin policy stops a page on one origin, meaning scheme plus host plus port, from reading a response from another. CORS, cross-origin resource sharing, is the mechanism by which a server opts in, using the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to name who may read it. For requests that are not simple, the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight asking what is permitted.

The point to make in an answer: CORS is a browser restriction protecting the user, not a server security feature. A server still needs its own authentication and authorisation, because anything outside a browser can call it freely.

Drill

  1. What is AJAX and what problem did it solve? Requesting data asynchronously after page load and updating part of the page; it removed the need for a full reload on every interaction.
  2. Differentiate JSON from XML. The table above.
  3. What is the same origin policy, and what is CORS? A browser rule preventing a page from reading responses from a different origin; CORS is the header-based mechanism by which a server permits named origins to do so.
  4. Write JavaScript to fetch JSON from /api/courses and display each course name in a list. fetch the URL, await or then the json, then loop creating an li per item with textContent and appending it, with a catch for the failure case.

t7.prompt: Usually a descriptive question rather than a coding one. Know what a framework buys you and what it costs.
t7.solution:
Why frameworks exist

  • Component model. The interface is built from reusable, self-contained pieces with their own markup, style and behaviour.
  • Declarative rendering. You describe what the interface should look like for a given state, and the framework works out the DOM changes, instead of you writing them by hand.
  • State management. A defined place for data to live and a defined way for changes to propagate.
  • Routing. Multiple views without a page reload.

And the cost, which a good answer names: a build step, a much larger JavaScript payload, a dependency tree to maintain, and worse performance on a slow phone or connection. For a page that is mostly static content, plain HTML is faster and simpler. Recognising when not to use a framework is what distinguishes a considered answer from a memorised one.

Rendering strategies

StrategyWhere the HTML is builtStrengthWeakness
Static siteAhead of time, at buildFastest, cheapest, most reliableContent cannot be personalised per request
Server side renderingOn the server, per requestGood first paint and search indexing; personalisedServer cost per request
Client side renderingIn the browser, by JavaScriptRich interaction after loadBlank page until the script loads and runs; harder to index

A single page application loads one document and then rewrites its content as the user navigates, using client side routing. The trade-off: navigation after load feels instant, but the first load is heavier and search engines and screen readers need extra care.

Drill

  1. State four benefits of using a front end framework, and two costs. The lists above.
  2. Differentiate server side rendering from client side rendering. The table, with the first paint and indexing consequences.
  3. What is a single page application, and what are its advantages and disadvantages? One document rewritten by JavaScript as the user navigates; fast transitions after load, at the cost of a heavier first load and more work for indexing and accessibility.

t8.prompt: REST, representational state transfer, is an architectural style for web APIs in which everything is a resource identified by a URL, and the HTTP method says what to do with it.
t8.solution:
The constraints

  • Client-server. The interface is separate from the storage and logic.
  • Stateless. Every request carries everything needed to understand it; the server stores no client context between requests.
  • Cacheable. Responses say whether they may be cached.
  • Uniform interface. Resources are identified by URL and manipulated through a standard set of methods.
  • Layered system. A client cannot tell whether it is connected to the server or to an intermediary.

Designing the endpoints

Method and pathDoesTypical response
GET /api/coursesList all courses200 with an array
GET /api/courses/csc311Fetch one course200, or 404 if absent
POST /api/coursesCreate a course201 with the new resource
PUT /api/courses/csc311Replace it entirely200 or 204
PATCH /api/courses/csc311Update part of it200
DELETE /api/courses/csc311Remove it204

The rule that earns the design mark: the URL names a thing, the method names the action. So /api/courses/csc311 with DELETE, never /api/deleteCourse?id=csc311. Use plural nouns, no verbs in paths, and nest only where there is a genuine containment relationship, such as /api/courses/csc311/materials.

Also worth naming: versioning, usually /api/v1/..., so a change does not break existing clients; pagination for large collections; and consistent error bodies so a client can handle failure programmatically rather than by reading prose.

REST against SOAP and GraphQL

SOAP is an older protocol using XML envelopes with a formal contract (WSDL) and built-in standards for security and transactions. It is heavier and stricter. GraphQL exposes a single endpoint and lets the client specify exactly which fields it wants, which solves over-fetching and under-fetching but moves complexity to the server. REST sits between them and is the default.

Drill

  1. What is REST and state four of its constraints? The definition and any four bullets.
  2. Design REST endpoints for a student records system. The table pattern applied to students, with plural nouns, the method carrying the action, and the appropriate status code for each.
  3. Differentiate REST from SOAP. REST is an architectural style over HTTP using URLs and methods with typically JSON payloads and no formal contract; SOAP is a protocol using XML envelopes with a WSDL contract and built-in standards, making it heavier but stricter.
  4. Why should a URL not contain a verb? Because the HTTP method already expresses the action, so putting it in the path duplicates it, breaks the uniform interface, and prevents caches and intermediaries from reasoning about the request.

t9.prompt: What actually happens on the server, and how the application reaches its data. This is where CSC311 meets DTS304, and saying so in an answer costs nothing and reads well.
t9.solution:
The request pipeline on the server

  1. Routing. Match the method and path to a handler.
  2. Middleware. Cross-cutting work applied to many routes: logging, parsing the body, authentication, rate limiting.
  3. Validation. Check the input, since it cannot be trusted whatever the client did.
  4. Business logic. The actual work.
  5. Data access. Query or update the database.
  6. Response. Serialise a result and set the status code and headers.

Connecting to a database

Two approaches. Writing SQL directly gives full control and predictable performance but more code. An ORM, object relational mapper, presents tables as objects, which is faster to write and portable between databases, at the cost of hidden queries that can perform badly, the classic case being the N+1 query problem where fetching a list then looping to fetch each item's relations issues one query per row.

Connection pooling is worth naming: opening a database connection is expensive, so a pool of open connections is kept and reused across requests.

The security rule that must appear in any answer touching database access: always use parameterised queries or prepared statements. Building SQL by concatenating user input is what creates SQL injection, and the fix is to send the query and the values separately so the input can never be parsed as SQL. This is the same point as DTS304 T26, and the two courses examine it identically.

SQL against NoSQL, briefly

Relational (SQL)Document (NoSQL)
StructureTables with a fixed schemaFlexible documents, usually JSON-like
RelationshipsJoins and foreign keysEmbedding or manual references
GuaranteesStrong, ACID transactionsOften eventual consistency, varies by product
Best forStructured, related data; anything financialVarying shapes, rapid iteration, very large scale
ExamplesMySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL ServerMongoDB, Firebase, DynamoDB

Drill

  1. Describe how a server processes an incoming HTTP request. The six pipeline steps above.
  2. What is middleware, with two examples? Code that runs between receiving a request and handling it, applied across many routes; for example authentication checks and request logging.
  3. Differentiate SQL from NoSQL databases and say when each suits. The table above.
  4. What is SQL injection and how is it prevented? Placing user input into a query so it is interpreted as SQL rather than data, letting an attacker change what the statement does; prevented by parameterised queries or prepared statements, plus input validation and least privilege on the database account.

t10.prompt: Authentication establishes who a user is; authorisation establishes what they may do. Authentication comes first and authorisation acts on its result.
t10.solution:
Handling passwords

Never store a password. Store a hash produced by a deliberately slow algorithm designed for the purpose, such as bcrypt or Argon2, with a per-user salt so that two users choosing the same password get different hashes and a precomputed rainbow table is useless. On login, hash the supplied password and compare hashes.

The reason a slow hash is used is a favourite follow-up: a fast hash such as MD5 or SHA-256 lets an attacker who steals the database test billions of guesses a second. Deliberately slow, memory-hard functions make that economically impractical while costing a legitimate login only a few milliseconds.

The attacks to name

AttackWhat it doesDefence
SQL injectionUser input is interpreted as SQL, altering the queryParameterised queries, validation, least privilege
Cross-site scripting (XSS)Attacker script runs in another user's browser, stealing cookies or altering the pageEscape output, use textContent, set a Content Security Policy, HttpOnly cookies
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)A user's browser is tricked into sending an authenticated request they did not intendAnti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, checking the origin
Man in the middleTraffic is intercepted or altered in transitHTTPS everywhere, HSTS
Brute force and credential stuffingGuessing passwords, or reusing ones leaked elsewhereRate limiting, lockouts, multi-factor authentication
Insecure direct object referenceChanging an id in a URL to read someone else's recordCheck on every request that this user may access this object

XSS and CSRF are constantly confused, so fix the difference with one line each: XSS abuses the user's trust in the site, by running attacker code inside it; CSRF abuses the site's trust in the user, by riding on credentials the browser sends automatically.

HTTPS

HTTP inside a TLS-encrypted channel, providing confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server through a certificate signed by a trusted authority. It is also a prerequisite for service workers, geolocation and several other browser features, so a progressive web app cannot exist without it.

Drill

  1. Differentiate authentication from authorisation. Verifying identity against determining permitted actions, in that order.
  2. How should passwords be stored, and why? As salted hashes from a deliberately slow, purpose-built function such as bcrypt or Argon2; the salt defeats precomputed tables and the slowness defeats mass offline guessing.
  3. Explain XSS and CSRF and distinguish them. The table rows plus the trust sentence.
  4. Name four web security threats and a defence for each. Any four rows of the table.

t11.prompt: How an application reaches its users, and why it might be slow when it does.
t11.solution:
Hosting models

ModelYou manageSuits
Shared hostingOnly your filesSmall static or PHP sites
Virtual private serverThe whole operating systemFull control, at the cost of administration
Platform as a serviceOnly your codeMost student and startup projects
Serverless functionsIndividual functions, billed per invocationAPIs with uneven traffic

Supporting pieces to name: a domain name resolved by DNS; a TLS certificate for HTTPS; a CDN, which caches static files at locations near the user and is the single biggest win for a Nigerian audience served from a distant origin; and CI/CD, where a push to the repository automatically runs tests and deploys.

Performance

  • Reduce payload. Minify CSS and JavaScript, compress with gzip or Brotli, and above all size images correctly and use a modern format.
  • Reduce requests. Bundle where sensible, and inline what is tiny.
  • Cache. Set far-future cache headers on versioned static files, and use a CDN.
  • Defer what is not needed immediately. Load scripts with defer, and lazy-load images below the fold.
  • Query efficiently. Index the columns you filter on and avoid the N+1 problem.

Images are almost always the answer to "why is this site slow", and they are also the easiest fix. An unresized photograph straight from a phone can be several megabytes, which on mobile data is the difference between a page that loads and a user who leaves.

Drill

  1. Differentiate shared hosting, a VPS and platform as a service. The table above.
  2. What is a CDN and why does it help? A network of servers caching static content close to users; it cuts latency by shortening the distance a request travels and reduces load on the origin.
  3. State five techniques for improving web performance. The five bullets.
  4. What is CI/CD? Continuous integration, where every push is automatically built and tested, and continuous deployment, where passing changes are automatically released, so that integration problems surface immediately rather than at the end.

t12.prompt: The comparison table is at R3. What follows is how to answer the question well rather than merely correctly.
t12.solution:
How mobile differs from the desktop web

A question sometimes asks what makes mobile development different. The honest list:

  • Constrained resources. Less memory, a slower processor, and a battery the application is competing for.
  • Unreliable connectivity. The application must behave sensibly with no network, not merely fail.
  • Small touch interface. Targets must be large enough for a finger, and there is no hover.
  • Interruption. A call, a notification or a lock can suspend the app at any moment, which is exactly what the life cycle in T13 exists to handle.
  • Permissions and privacy. Access to camera, location, contacts and storage must be requested and can be refused.
  • Fragmentation. Many screen sizes, densities and operating system versions, which matters especially in a market where older Android devices are common.

That fragmentation point is worth making concrete for a Nigerian context: targeting only the newest Android version excludes a large share of real users, so a sensible minimum SDK and testing on a low-end device are engineering decisions, not afterthoughts.

Drill

  1. Compare native, hybrid and progressive web applications under performance, cost, device access and distribution. Table R3, closing with a justified recommendation.
  2. State five ways mobile development differs from web development. The list above.
  3. What is a progressive web app and what three things does it require? A website that behaves like an installed app; a service worker, a web app manifest, and HTTPS.
  4. When would you choose native over cross-platform? When performance is critical, when the app needs deep or early access to platform features, or when the platform's own look and feel matters to the product. Otherwise cross-platform delivers both platforms from one codebase for less.

t13.prompt: Close to a guaranteed question wherever Android is taught, because it is a fixed list of callbacks in a fixed order.
t13.solution:
The Android activity life cycle

CallbackCalled whenWhat belongs here
onCreate()The activity is first createdBuild the interface, bind data, restore saved state. Called once per creation
onStart()The activity becomes visibleStart work that should run while visible
onResume()The activity is in the foreground and interactiveStart animations, acquire the camera or sensors
onPause()Another activity is coming to the foregroundRelease the camera, pause animations. Keep it fast; the next activity waits on it
onStop()The activity is no longer visibleSave persistent data, release heavier resources
onRestart()A stopped activity is about to start againRe-acquire what onStop released
onDestroy()The activity is being destroyedFinal cleanup
Launch:            onCreate → onStart → onResume
Another app opens: onPause → onStop
Return to it:      onRestart → onStart → onResume
Back button:       onPause → onStop → onDestroy
Rotate the screen: onPause → onStop → onDestroy → onCreate → onStart → onResume

That last line is the discriminating detail. A rotation destroys and recreates the activity, which is why unsaved state disappears when a student rotates their phone, and why onSaveInstanceState() exists to preserve it. Volunteer that example and the answer is clearly understood rather than recited.

The four Android application components are worth naming alongside: Activity, one screen; Service, background work with no interface; Broadcast Receiver, responding to system-wide announcements; and Content Provider, sharing data between applications. An Intent is the message that starts or connects them, and is explicit when it names its target component and implicit when it merely describes an action for the system to match.

Drill

  1. List the Android activity life cycle callbacks in order and state what each is for. The table above.
  2. Which callbacks run when the user rotates the device, and why does that matter? The full destroy and recreate sequence; it matters because in-memory state is lost unless it is saved in onSaveInstanceState or held outside the activity.
  3. Name the four Android application components. Activity, Service, Broadcast Receiver, Content Provider.
  4. Differentiate an explicit from an implicit intent. An explicit intent names the exact component to start; an implicit intent describes an action and lets the system choose a component that can handle it.

t14.prompt: What a mobile application does with data, and what it does when the network is not there. This is the topic where your own site is a working case study.
t14.solution:
Storage options

OptionHoldsUse for
Key-value store, such as SharedPreferencesSmall primitivesSettings, flags, the last screen opened
Local database, such as SQLite or RoomStructured recordsAnything queried, listed or filtered offline
FilesImages, documents, cachesDownloaded media, exports
Remote APIThe authoritative dataAnything shared between users or devices

Working offline

The standard pattern is cache first, then network: show what is stored locally immediately, request fresh data in the background, and update the view when it arrives. On the web the same thing is done by a service worker, a script that sits between the page and the network and can serve cached responses when there is no connection.

Synchronisation raises the hard question: if the same record was changed locally and remotely, which wins? Strategies to name are last-write-wins, which is simple and can lose data; keeping both versions for the user to resolve; and merging by field where the data allows it.

You have an unusually good example of offline design to cite, and it is worth citing because it shows a decision rather than a technique: this study guide is built so every course page is entirely self-contained with relative links, so the folder works from a USB stick with the connection off, while the two features that genuinely need the network, uploading and the assistant, degrade honestly by saying so instead of failing silently. That last phrase, degrade honestly, is the principle an examiner is looking for.

Permissions

Modern Android requests dangerous permissions, namely camera, location, contacts, microphone and storage, at run time rather than at install, and the user can refuse or later revoke them. Two consequences for design: request a permission at the moment it is needed with an explanation, not all of them at launch, and always handle refusal gracefully, since an application that crashes or becomes useless when a permission is denied is a defect.

Drill

  1. Name four mobile data storage options and say what each suits. The table above.
  2. How should an application behave with no network connection? Serve cached data immediately, queue any changes for later synchronisation, tell the user clearly which features are unavailable, and retry when connectivity returns.
  3. What is a service worker? A script running separately from the page that intercepts network requests, allowing responses to be cached and served offline, and enabling background sync and push notifications.
  4. Why are run time permissions better than install time permissions? Because the user sees the request in the context where it is needed, can judge it against a visible purpose, can grant a subset, and can revoke it later, which gives real control rather than a single all-or-nothing decision at install.

t15.prompt: The last of the mobile topics, and usually the shortest question.
t15.solution:
Interface principles for a small screen

  • Touch targets of roughly 48 density-independent pixels, since a fingertip is not a cursor.
  • Thumb reach. Primary actions belong in the lower portion of the screen, where a thumb naturally falls.
  • One primary action per screen, with secondary actions subordinated.
  • Feedback for every action, since without a hover state the user needs confirmation that a tap registered.
  • Density independence. Size in dp and sp, not pixels, so the layout holds across screen densities.
  • Accessibility. Content descriptions on icons, adequate contrast, and respecting the system font size.

Publishing

  1. Build a signed release: a signed APK or, for Google Play, an Android App Bundle.
  2. Prepare the store listing: title, description, screenshots, an icon, and a privacy policy.
  3. Set the content rating, the target audience and the countries of distribution.
  4. Upload, roll out to internal or closed testing first, then to production.
  5. After release, monitor crash reports and reviews and ship updates as new versions.

The signing key deserves its own sentence, because losing it is unrecoverable: an update must be signed with the same key as the original, so a lost key means the application can never be updated and must be republished under a new identity, losing its users and reviews.

Drill

  1. State five principles of mobile user interface design. The list above.
  2. Describe the steps to publish an Android application. The five numbered steps.
  3. Why must the signing key be kept safe? Because updates must be signed with the same key as the original release; if it is lost the application cannot be updated at all and must be republished as a new listing.
  4. Why size in dp rather than px? Because a density-independent pixel is scaled by the device's screen density, so an element keeps the same physical size across devices, whereas a fixed pixel size shrinks on a high density screen.

t16.prompt: The professional practice around the code, which project marking schemes almost always include and most students almost always neglect.
t16.solution:
Git, the commands and the concepts

CommandDoes
git init, git cloneStart a repository, or copy an existing one
git add, git commitStage changes, then record them with a message
git push, git pullSend commits to the remote, or fetch and merge from it
git branch, git checkout, git mergeCreate a line of work, switch to it, and combine it back
git log, git diff, git statusInspect history, changes and the current state

The concepts behind them: a repository is the project with its full history; a commit is a snapshot with a message and a parent; a branch is a movable pointer to a commit, letting work proceed in parallel; a merge conflict happens when two branches change the same lines and Git cannot decide, so a human must.

For a group project, the argument for version control is not "backup". It is that several people can work at once without overwriting each other, every change is attributable to a person and a reason, and any broken state can be traced and reverted. Marking schemes that mention teamwork are usually looking for exactly that, and a repository with commits from every member is direct evidence of it.

Testing

LevelChecks
UnitOne function or component in isolation
IntegrationThat parts work together, for example a route against its database
End to endA whole user journey through the real interface
User acceptanceThat real users agree it does what was asked

Also worth naming: cross-browser and cross-device testing, which for this course means at minimum one real low-end Android phone rather than only a desktop browser window resized.

Documentation

A README that states what the project is, how to install and run it, what environment variables it needs, and how it is deployed. If the project has an API, document each endpoint with its method, path, parameters and an example response. Documentation is cheap to write and is frequently a named line on the marking scheme.

Drill

  1. What is version control and why is it essential for team projects? A system recording every change with its author and reason, allowing parallel work, attribution and reversion to any earlier state.
  2. Differentiate a branch from a merge, and explain a merge conflict. A branch is an independent line of development; a merge combines two lines; a conflict arises when both changed the same lines and the tool cannot choose, requiring manual resolution.
  3. Name four levels of testing and what each checks. The table above.
  4. What should a project README contain? What the project does, how to install and run it, its configuration and environment requirements, how to deploy it, and how to use its API if it has one.

t17.prompt: No past paper was supplied, so this is advice rather than a predicted question. It is here because in a build-assessed course the project usually decides the grade, and the failure modes are predictable.
t17.solution:
What actually loses marks

  • Nothing deployed. A project that runs only on the developer's laptop cannot be marked properly, and a demonstration that fails because of a local dependency is a self-inflicted wound. Deploy early, even when it is ugly, then keep deploying.
  • No data. An application demonstrated with one record looks unfinished. Seed realistic content before the demonstration.
  • Broken on a phone. In a course with "mobile" in its title, a layout that breaks at 360px wide is the worst possible defect. Test at that width from the first week.
  • No error states. Every load has three states, namely loading, empty and failed, and most student projects implement only success. Handling all three is the cheapest way to look finished.
  • An uneven repository. If the marking scheme includes teamwork, a repository where one member made every commit is evidence against the group, whatever the report claims.
  • Left to the end. The last week is for polish and rehearsal, not for building. Whatever is unfinished then stays unfinished.

A sensible order of work

  1. Agree the one thing the application does, and write it in a sentence. Scope creep is the commonest cause of an unfinished project.
  2. Sketch the screens on paper. It takes an hour and saves a week.
  3. Design the data model first, using DTS304: entities, relationships, keys, normalized to 3NF. Everything else is easier once this is right, and changing it later is expensive.
  4. Build one complete vertical slice end to end, from interface through API to database and back, before building anything else. It proves the whole stack works.
  5. Deploy that slice. Now deployment is solved while the project is still small.
  6. Add the remaining features one at a time, deploying each.
  7. Spend the last week on error states, mobile layout, seeding data, the README and rehearsing the demonstration.

Demonstrating it

Prepare a path through the application that shows every feature in a few minutes, and rehearse it. Have the deployed URL open and ready in case the local copy misbehaves, and have screenshots in case the network does. Be able to answer "why did you choose this stack" in two sentences, because it is the most common question and it is testing whether the choice was a decision or an accident.

One genuine advantage to use: you have already deployed a production site with an API, file uploads, offline support and a database-backed assistant. When a design question comes up in this course, answer from that experience rather than from a textbook. Concrete beats general in a viva every time.

w1.prompt: Show the basic HTML structure and explain its components. (asked 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25)
w1.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Page title</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Heading</h1>
<p>Content goes here.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • <!DOCTYPE html>: declares the document as HTML5, so the browser uses standards mode.
  • <html>: the root element that wraps the whole page; lang states the language.
  • <head>: metadata not shown on the page: character set, title, links to CSS, viewport.
  • <title>: the name shown on the browser tab.
  • <body>: everything visible: headings, paragraphs, images, links, forms.

w2.prompt: Describe HTML as a web language, with emphasis on its syntax. (all three years)
w2.solution:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language for creating web pages. It is not a programming language: it has no logic or variables. Instead it describes the structure and meaning of content using tags that the browser renders.

Syntax. Content is wrapped in elements. An element is usually an opening tag, content, and a closing tag: <p>text</p>. Tags are written in angle brackets and most come in pairs, the closing one carrying a slash. Elements can nest and carry attributes as name-value pairs in the opening tag: <a href="page.html">link</a>. Some elements are empty (no content, no closing tag), such as <img> and <br>. Tag names are case-insensitive, attribute values are quoted.

w3.prompt: Explain the concept of semantic markup in HTML and give its advantages. Also: the three main components used for structuring web pages. (2023/24, 2024/25)
w3.solution:
Semantic markup means using HTML elements that describe the meaning of the content, not just its appearance: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <footer>, instead of wrapping everything in a plain <div>.

Advantages: better accessibility (screen readers understand the structure), better SEO (search engines weight meaningful tags), readable and maintainable code, and consistent structure across browsers.

The three components used to structure a web page: HTML for structure and content, CSS for presentation and layout, and JavaScript for behaviour and interactivity. Example: HTML lays out a form, CSS styles it, JavaScript validates it before submit.

w4.prompt: Discuss the components of a typical web-based application architecture. (all three years)
w4.solution:
A web application is usually a three-tier architecture:

  • Client (presentation) tier: the browser, running HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It renders the interface and takes user input.
  • Application (logic) tier: the web/application server that holds the business logic, processes requests and generates responses (PHP, Node.js, Python, Java).
  • Data tier: the database server that stores and retrieves data (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB).

Supporting components: the web server (serves pages and routes requests), the HTTP protocol connecting client and server, and often an API layer between the logic and data tiers. The browser sends a request over HTTP, the application tier processes it (querying the data tier as needed), and returns a response the browser renders.

w5.prompt: Write a short note on Application Programming Interface. (all three years)
w5.solution:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of definitions and rules that lets one piece of software talk to another. It exposes certain functions or data while hiding the internal implementation, so a client can use a service by calling its endpoints without knowing how it works inside.

On the web, a web API is typically accessed over HTTP: the client sends a request to a URL (endpoint) and receives structured data back, usually as JSON. REST is the common style. Example: a weather API where GET /weather?city=Ibadan returns today's forecast as JSON. APIs enable reuse, integration between systems, and separation of front end from back end.

w6.prompt: List and explain any three front-end technologies/languages, and any three back-end technologies/languages. (front end 2022/23, 2024/25; back end 2023/24, 2024/25)
w6.solution:
Front-end (runs in the browser, builds what the user sees):

  • HTML: structures the content of the page.
  • CSS: styles and lays out that content (colour, spacing, responsiveness).
  • JavaScript: adds interactivity and dynamic behaviour; frameworks such as React or Vue build on it.

Back-end (runs on the server, handles logic and data):

  • PHP: a server-side scripting language for dynamic pages.
  • Python (with Django/Flask) or Node.js (JavaScript): handle requests and business logic.
  • SQL: queries and manages the database (with a DBMS such as MySQL).

w7.prompt: List and explain the different types of application development environments. (all three years)
w7.solution:
These are the separate environments a piece of software passes through before release:

EnvironmentPurpose
Developmentwhere developers write and change code, on their own machines
Testing / QAwhere the software is tested for bugs, separate from development
Staginga near-exact copy of production, for final checks before release
Productionthe live environment that real users access

Keeping them separate means untested code never reaches users, and a bug can be caught in testing or staging rather than in production.

w8.prompt: State and discuss the objectives of Rapid Application Development. (all three years)
w8.solution:
RAD is a development methodology that favours fast, iterative building with working prototypes over long up-front planning. Its objectives:

  • Speed: deliver working software quickly through rapid prototyping.
  • User involvement: get continuous user feedback on prototypes, so the product matches real needs.
  • Flexibility: accommodate changing requirements late in the process.
  • Reuse: use existing components and tools to cut development time.
  • Reduced cost and risk: catch problems early on small increments rather than at the end.

w9.prompt: Differentiate between a web designer and a web developer who use HTML, CSS and JavaScript. (2022/23, 2024/25)
w9.solution:
Web designerWeb developer
Focuslook, feel, user experiencefunction, logic, how it works
Main toolsHTML, CSS, design toolsHTML, CSS, JavaScript and back-end languages
Skillslayout, colour, typography, UXprogramming, data, APIs, debugging
Outputthe visual interface and stylethe working, interactive application

In short: the designer decides how the site looks and feels; the developer makes it work. There is overlap in HTML and CSS, but JavaScript logic and back-end code are the developer's domain.

w10.prompt: Compare Internet and Web; compare Web Browser and Web Server. Describe the web application development cycle. (2022/23, 2024/25)
w10.solution:
Internet vs Web: the Internet is the global network of interconnected computers (the infrastructure). The Web (WWW) is one service that runs on top of it: a system of linked hypertext documents accessed over HTTP. The Internet also carries email, file transfer and more; the Web is just one of them.

Web browser vs web server: the browser is client software that requests and displays web pages (Chrome, Firefox). The server is software (and the machine) that stores pages and responds to browser requests over HTTP. The browser asks; the server answers.

Web application development cycle: requirement analysis, then design (interface and architecture), then development (front and back end), then testing, then deployment to production, then maintenance and updates. It is iterative: feedback loops back into design.

w11.prompt: Using the default link element, give two examples of each: (i) link to a JavaScript function, (ii) link to a resource on an external site, (iii) link to a separate page on the same site. (2023/24, 2024/25)
w11.solution:
The default link element is the anchor, <a>. What changes is the href.

<!-- (i) link that runs a JavaScript function -->
<a href="javascript:doSave()">Save</a>
<a href="#" onclick="doSave(); return false;">Save</a>
<!-- (ii) link to a resource on an external site (absolute URL) -->
<a href="https://www.example.edu">University</a>
<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org">MDN</a>
<!-- (iii) link to another page on the same site (relative URL) -->
<a href="about.html">About</a>
<a href="courses/csc311.html">CSC311</a>

Note the pattern: a JavaScript link calls code, an external link needs the full https:// address, and a same-site link uses a relative path (W12).

w12.prompt: With respect to page resources, differentiate between URL relative and absolute referencing. (2023/24, 2024/25)
w12.solution:
Absolute referencing gives the complete address, including the scheme and domain: https://site.com/img/logo.png. It points to the same place no matter where the referring page sits, and is needed for resources on another site.

Relative referencing gives a path relative to the current page's location: img/logo.png, or ../index.html to go up a folder. It stays valid if the whole site is moved or renamed, and is shorter, so it is preferred for links within the same site.

Rule of thumb: relative for your own site's resources, absolute for external ones. This is exactly why this study guide uses relative links, so it runs from a folder offline.

w13.prompt: Distinguish GET and POST; discuss the methods of passing information in HTTP; explain the mechanism to monitor a user's state across multiple requests, and the risk if it is not done. (2022/23, 2023/24)
w13.solution:
GETPOST
Data goes inthe URL query string (visible)the request body (not in the URL)
Data sizelimited (URL length)effectively unlimited
Caching / bookmarkingyesno
Use forretrieving data, safe searchessubmitting sensitive or large data (login, upload)

Passing information in HTTP: the query string (GET), the request body (POST), HTTP headers, cookies, and URL path parameters.

State across requests. HTTP is stateless: each request is independent, so the server does not remember the last one. To track a user, use sessions (a session ID stored in a cookie identifies the user's server-side data) and cookies. Without this, the server cannot tell one user from another between pages: a logged-in user would appear logged out on the next page, and, worse, requests could be misattributed, allowing unauthorised access to another user's data.

w14.prompt: Design a login page: a username text field, a password field, a submit and a reset button, submitting to "Servers/regServer" for database authentication, with the field contents not appended to the URL, and with labels. (2022/23)
w14.solution:
The key mark is method="post": that is what keeps the username and password out of the URL (a GET form would append them, exposing the password).

<form action="Servers/regServer" method="post">
<label for="user">Username:</label>
<input type="text" id="user" name="user">
<label for="pass">Password:</label>
<input type="password" id="pass" name="pass">
<button type="submit">Login</button>
<button type="reset">Reset</button>
</form>
  • method="post" puts the data in the request body, not the URL.
  • type="password" masks the input; each <label for> matches an input id.
  • type="reset" clears the form; type="submit" sends it to the action URL.

w15.prompt: Write the HTML tags for: an ordered list of five names and matric numbers in a table with headings; and an index page whose headings contain your course level, serving as hyperlinks that reveal the 300L courses. (2022/23, 2023/24)
w15.solution:
Names and matric numbers in a table:

<table border="1">
<tr><th>S/N</th><th>Name</th><th>Matric Number</th></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>Ada Obi</td><td>CSC/2022/001</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>Bola Eze</td><td>CSC/2022/002</td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>Chidi Musa</td><td>CSC/2022/003</td></tr>
<tr><td>4</td><td>Dami Okon</td><td>CSC/2022/004</td></tr>
<tr><td>5</td><td>Efe Ali</td><td>CSC/2022/005</td></tr>
</table>

Index page with heading links to the 300L courses:

<h1>300 Level Computer Science</h1>
<ul>
<li><a href="csc311.html">CSC311 Web Technologies</a></li>
<li><a href="csc325.html">CSC325 Compiler Construction</a></li>
<li><a href="csc328.html">CSC328 Discrete Structures</a></li>
</ul>

If the question specifically wants an ordered list, swap <ul> for <ol>, which numbers the items automatically.

w16.prompt: (a) Show how to set the minimum and maximum values for an input in HTML5. (b) Create a table with 100% width and a vertical scroll inside the table body. (2023/24)
w16.solution:
(a) Min and max on a number input:

<input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="60">

The min and max attributes bound the value; the browser rejects anything outside the range on submit. (For a range slider, use type="range" with the same attributes.)

(b) 100% wide table whose body scrolls: make the header and body block-level so the body can take a fixed height and scroll.

<style>
table   { width: 100%; }
tbody   { display: block; max-height: 150px; overflow-y: auto; }
thead, tbody tr { display: table; width: 100%; table-layout: fixed; }
</style>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Name</th><th>Score</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Ada</td><td>70</td></tr>
<!-- more rows; the body scrolls past 150px -->
</tbody>
</table>

w17.prompt: Explain how to use the Web Share API for native share options, stating its features and limitations. (2023/24)
w17.solution:
The Web Share API lets a web page invoke the device's native share dialog (the same sheet apps use), through navigator.share():

<button onclick="share()">Share</button>
<script>
function share() {
if (navigator.share) {
navigator.share({
title: 'CSC311',
text:  'Study guide',
url:   'https://example.com'
});
}
}
</script>

Features: uses the OS share sheet, so the user can share to any installed app; takes title, text and URL (and files). Limitations: it must be triggered by a user gesture (a click), it requires a secure context (HTTPS), and support is limited mainly to mobile browsers, so a fallback is needed on unsupported desktops (hence the if (navigator.share) check).
